TASK: The maintenance technician was swapping the transfer hose on the parts washer at the quick disconnect fitting. The task was a response to a fault, jam or alarm. Stage of the task: planned maintenance. Method in effect: WI-905 Parts Washer Hose Replacement. The task was being performed as written. Equipment involved: Parts washer PW-02 transfer line at the quick disconnect fitting. Equipment state at the time: pressurized, hot and energized. Equipment condition: known fault already reported. Detail: The fitting had been weeping at the seal for about two shifts and was on the maintenance list. PPE in use: safety glasses, chemical gloves and a face shield. This differed from the PPE specified for the task.

SEQUENCE: The event was witnessed by at least one other person. Immediately before the event: kneeling at the front of the washer with both hands on the quick disconnect and the left forearm resting across the frame about 8 inches below the fitting. Body position at the moment: kneeling. At the moment of the event: the disconnect released under residual pressure and heated wash solution sprayed downward across the inner left forearm between the glove cuff and the sleeve. Immediately after the event: the technician pulled back from the machine, called out to Michael at the next bay, and walked to the emergency shower about 20 feet away.

MECHANISM: Source: Heated caustic wash solution from the parts washer transfer line at the quick disconnect fitting. Magnitude: About 180 degrees Fahrenheit at roughly 4 percent caustic. Contact lasted a few seconds. Isolation state: the line was drained but still pressurized and isolation is not required by the written method. Point of contact: inner left forearm from the wrist to below the elbow. Force applied from above.

CONDITIONS: Difference from a normal run of this task: The line normally depressurizes overnight, but this swap was done mid shift with the washer still warm. Conditions at the point of injury: restricted working space and hot. Detail: The space in front of the washer is tight and the technician had to kneel with the forearm on the frame to reach the fitting. The event occurred in the first half of the shift. No overtime was being worked. It happened within roughly half an hour in. The maintenance technician had performed this task before. A known hazard, prior near miss, open action or risk assessment covers this task. Detail: The weeping fitting had been reported on the previous shift and a work order was open at the time of the event. A guard, interlock, barrier or control was bypassed, missing, defeated or ineffective. Detail: Sleeve protection is available in stores but is not listed in the written method for this task, so none was worn. Stop-work opportunity: The swap could have waited until end of shift when the washer had cooled and the line had depressurized.

IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: At the scene, an emergency shower was used and a sterile dressing was applied. Detail: Irrigated at the emergency shower for about 15 minutes. This was given by the site emergency response team. Notified: the supervisor, EHS and the site emergency response team. This happened immediately. Afterwards, the equipment was locked and tagged out and the area was barriered off. Work at the location stopped. The maintenance technician was sent to an emergency room for evaluation.
